digest.question: Why does an epidemic end before everyone has caught it?

hookResult.text: An epidemic can end while many people are still well: it fades once too few are left for the ill to keep it spreading, not once everyone has been ill.

counterfactual.prompt: What if the ill stayed infectious twice as long?
counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: Ill twice as long, each person passes the illness to more of the town: by day 200 the other town has more than 100 fewer people still well.

beginner.text: A few ill people arrive in a town where everyone else is well. The illness passes on when the ill meet the well, and in time the ill are removed: they recover, are isolated or die. Watch it spread, peak and fade. When it is over, many people never caught it.
beginner.analogy: Like a fire in a dry field that burns out with patches left unburnt, once the flames are too far apart to jump.

intermediate.text: The infection rate sets how often a meeting of an ill person and a well one passes the illness on. The epidemic grows while the ill infect others faster than they are removed, and fades once too few people are still well for that to go on. It ends with people who were never ill.

advanced.text: In the paper's special case of constant rates, x counts those still well, y the ill and z the removed; κ is the rate of infection and l the rate of removal. x only falls, and it stops falling once y has fallen to nothing, which happens while x is still above 0.
advanced.equation: dx/dt = −κxy,  dy/dt = κxy − ly,  dz/dt = ly

beginner.text: Everyone in the town is in one of three groups: still well, ill, or removed. The ill can pass the illness on. The removed cannot: they have recovered, been isolated or died. No one moves back, so people only go from well, to ill, to removed.
beginner.analogy: Like guests at a party who arrive, dance and leave: no one who has left comes back in.

intermediate.text: The paper sorts a population into those not yet infected, the infected, and those removed by recovery, isolation or death. Removal takes the ill out of the spread: the faster it is, the shorter each person's illness, and the fewer are ill at once.

advanced.text: Each of the y ill is removed at rate l, so an illness lasts 1/l days on average. x + y + z = N stays constant: no one enters or leaves the town, and people move only from x to y to z.
advanced.equation: dz/dt = ly,  x + y + z = N

beginner.text: Whether an epidemic starts depends on how many people the ill can meet. In a big town, each ill person passes the illness to more than one other before being removed, and it spreads. In a small one, each passes it to fewer than one, and it fades out.
beginner.analogy: Like a rumour in a small village: if each person tells fewer than one other, it dies out.

intermediate.text: The paper finds a threshold: an epidemic grows only if more people can catch the illness than the rate of removal divided by the rate of infection. In this world that is about 333 people at the start. Remove the ill fast enough, or have few enough people, and the illness fades however it begins.

advanced.text: dy/dt = (κx − l) y, so the ill grow only while x is above l/κ, the threshold. At the start nearly everyone is still well, so an epidemic takes off only in a town of more than l/κ people.
advanced.equation: dy/dt = (κx − l) y,  growing only while x > l/κ

counterfactual.prompt: What if ten times as many were ill at the start?
counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: Ten times as many ill at the start barely moves the end: in none of 20 towns does the other have more than 10 fewer people still well at day 150.

beginner.text: Start with five ill people, or fifty: with more, the epidemic comes sooner, but it ends in nearly the same place. How many escape is set by how easily the illness passes on, how fast the ill are removed and how many live in the town, much more than by how it began.
beginner.analogy: Like a ball rolled into a valley: start it higher or lower on the slope, and it still comes to rest near the bottom.

intermediate.text: How many are never ill is set mostly by the two rates and the town's size. More ill people at the start bring the peak sooner, but change the end by only a few people, as long as they are a small part of the town.

advanced.text: With no one removed at the start, the run ends where x∞ = x₀ exp(−κ(N − x∞)/l), a consequence of the paper's equations. x₀ = N − y₀ enters only through a factor close to 1 while y₀ is small next to N.

counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: In a town of 2,000 the illness reaches nearly everyone: by day 150 it has more than 20 fewer people still well than this town of 1,000, not more.

beginner.text: Twice the people means each ill person meets twice as many who are still well, so the illness spreads faster and further. A bigger town ends with fewer people who never caught it: not just a smaller share, but fewer people.
beginner.analogy: Like a spark in a packed hall rather than a half-empty one.

intermediate.text: New infections come from meetings of the ill and the well, so they grow with the number of people. In a town of 2,000 the epidemic is far above its threshold: it reaches more of the town, and leaves fewer people untouched, counted in people, not only as a share.

advanced.text: κxy doubles when x does, so at the start the ill grow at κN − l, the infection term twice as large in a town twice the size. The end, x∞ = x₀ exp(−κ(N − x∞)/l), falls fast as N grows.

limits.text: A teaching adaptation of the paper's special case, in which the rates of infection and removal are constants. The paper's general theory, where both may change with how long someone has been ill, is not shown.
The paper counts people per unit of area, a density. This world counts the people in one town, the same model with the town's area fixed.
Every value here, of the two rates, the town's size and the ill at the start, is a teaching choice, not the paper's.
The paper compares its theory with the deaths from plague in Bombay in 1905 and 1906. This world reproduces neither that comparison nor any of the paper's data.

anchors.need: The paper's comparison of its theory with the deaths from plague in Bombay in 1905 and 1906.

limits.text: The model has no chance in it: a town with the same values always runs the same way. So each level's statement is checked on the world's own values and on 19 others, each within a tenth of them, not on 20 seeds.
